title: The backup that wasn't
summary: A bad deploy corrupts production data. Your replicas have the corruption too. What do you restore from?

statement.situation: Your primary database holds 150 GB and takes about 1,000 writes/s. At some point a bad deploy starts writing corrupt data. It is noticed five minutes later. Because replicas faithfully copy everything, they now hold the corruption as well. Recovery means restoring from a backup — if you have a good one. On a previous project, a nightly backup job had been failing silently for months.
symptoms: Data is wrong, and failing over to a replica doesn't help
Nobody knows when the last good backup was taken
Restoring takes much longer than anyone assumed
requirements: Lose no more than 8 minutes of writes (≈ 480,000 writes)
Restore service within 30 minutes of starting recovery
Survive the case where backup jobs have been silently failing
constraints: Restore speed and data size are fixed by your infrastructure
You decide what to back up, how often, and how you know it works

learningObjectives: Why replication is not a backup
RPO and RTO as design inputs
Verifying that backups can be restored

references.title: GitLab: postmortem of database outage of January 31
PostgreSQL: continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery
PostgreSQL: reliability and the write-ahead log

scenarios.name: Corruption at t=1000 s, noticed 5 minutes later
scenarios.description: 1,800 req/s (≈ 1,000 writes/s). A bad write begins at t=1000 s and is detected at t=1300 s.

successCriteria.label: At most 8 minutes of writes lost
Service restored within 30 minutes of starting recovery
Also survives backup jobs that were silently failing
